lms.title: Arbitrage, Replication, and the Cost of Carry in Pricing Derivatives
lms.summary: No-arbitrage pricing, replication, and how carry costs and benefits set forward prices.

los.statement: Explain how the concepts of arbitrage and replication are used in pricing derivatives.

inline.t: Arbitrage
is a riskless profit with no net investment. If two portfolios have identical future payoffs, they must cost the same today (
law of one price
). Derivatives are priced so that no arbitrage exists.
Replication
: a long forward can be replicated by borrowing money to buy the underlying and holding it until expiry. So the forward price must equal the cost of that strategy.
F₀(T) = S₀ × (1 + r)^T   (no carry costs or benefits)
A share trades at ₹1,000, pays no dividend, and the one-year rate is 6%. F₀ = 1,000 × 1.06 =
. If the forward traded at ₹1,080, sell the forward, borrow ₹1,000, buy the share; at expiry deliver the share for ₹1,080 and repay ₹1,060: riskless profit ₹20.
Holding the underlying can generate
benefits
(dividends, coupons, convenience yield) and
costs
(storage, insurance). Benefits lower the forward price; costs raise it.
F₀(T) = [S₀ − PV(benefits) + PV(costs)] × (1 + r)^T  ·  continuous: F₀ = S₀ e^{(r + c − i)T}
Gold spot ₹70,000 per 10 g, storage costs with a PV of ₹500, rate 5%, one year. F₀ = (70,000 + 500) × 1.05 =
Risk-neutral pricing: the forward price does not depend on the expected future spot price or on investors' risk preferences, only on spot, rates and carry.
Arbitrageurs are the people who notice the same mango is ₹40 at one stall and ₹50 at the next. After a few minutes, both stalls charge ₹45.
F₀ = (S₀ − PV benefits + PV costs) × (1 + r)^T

lms.title: Valuing a Derivative Using a One-Period Binomial Model
lms.summary: Up and down moves, the hedge ratio, risk-neutral probabilities and option values.

los.statement: Explain how to value a derivative using a one-period binomial model.
Describe the concept of risk neutrality in derivatives pricing.

inline.t: The underlying moves to S⁺ = S₀u or S⁻ = S₀d in one period. Work out the option payoff in each state, then discount the
risk-neutral
expected payoff at the risk-free rate.
Buying h shares and selling one call gives a riskless portfolio. In the example h = 20 ÷ 40 = 0.5: hold half a share per call written.
π is
not

the real-world probability of an up move. It is the probability that makes the underlying earn the risk-free rate. Because the option can be replicated, its price does not depend on investors' risk preferences or real-world probabilities.
A put uses the same π: p₀ = [πp⁺ + (1 − π)p⁻] ÷ (1 + r). In the example p⁺ = 0, p⁻ = 20, so p₀ = 0.375 × 20 ÷ 1.05 = ₹7.14. Check with parity: 11.90 + 95.24 − 100 = 7.14.
Risk-neutral probability is a polite fiction, like a GPS saying '5 minutes away' in Mumbai traffic. It gets you the right price even if it isn't how the world really works.
π = (1 + r − d)/(u − d) · Value = [π V⁺ + (1 − π) V⁻]/(1 + r) · h = ΔV/ΔS
